analysis.one_liner: Bans for-profit corporations from running political action committees for elections.
analysis.headline: The bill got a hearing referral but never a vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal election law so that only nonprofit corporations could establish and operate political action committees, the traditional corporate checkbooks for giving directly to candidates. For-profit corporate PACs would have to shut down and disburse their funds within a year. It would also stop corporate PACs from soliciting donations from shareholders, limiting solicitation to executives and administrative personnel. It would not touch super PACs or other outside spending.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, candidates who rely on small donors rather than corporate money, and anyone concerned that companies use their PACs to buy access to the lawmakers who regulate them. When a corporate PAC gives, the money comes from pooled company funds solicited from employees and is steered with the approval of company leadership, giving incumbent officeholders a steady stream of industry cash.

how_it_helps.text: Only nonprofit corporations could establish or operate a corporate political action committee, closing the door for all for-profit companies [S3].
Existing corporate PACs would have to terminate and disburse their entire balance within one year of enactment [S3].
Corporate PACs could no longer solicit contributions from stockholders and their families, only from executive and administrative personnel [S3].
The same limits would apply to PACs set up by government contractors, extending the ban to companies seeking federal contracts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit corporations and their PACs, which would lose the dedicated vehicle they use to bundle money for members of Congress and party committees, plus the fundraising professionals and party operations that depend on that money.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves super PACs untouched, which can raise unlimited corporate money for independent spending; banning traditional corporate PACs would not stop corporations from spending on elections through those channels [S3].

Corporate PAC giving is a relatively small slice of campaign money, so the bill would not end corporate influence over elections; company executives could still give personally and corporate treasuries could still fund super PACs [S3].
Banning the traditional PAC could push corporate political activity into less visible channels, such as leadership PACs and executive donations, where the corporate source is harder to trace.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill takes a real, if partial, step: it shuts down the vehicle through which companies pool and steer money directly to the members of Congress who regulate them. Its weakness is that it does nothing about super PACs or unlimited independent spending, so the largest corporate money would continue as before. It would have changed the texture of congressional fundraising but not ended corporate influence.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 2023, referred to the House Committee on House Administration twelve days later, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Josh Harder introduced the Ban Corporate PACs Act on October 12, 2023, joined by his cosponsor [S1].
On October 25, 2023 the bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration, which was its last action [S5].
The bill had 2 cosponsors and never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate PACs and the incumbent members of Congress they fund are better off; the bill died without a vote, so the traditional corporate fundraising channel remains open.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporate PACs and the members they fund

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on October 25, 2023 and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, so no roll-call split exists; its three supporters were all Democrats, and the Republican-controlled committee took no action.

industries.note: These companies would lose the PAC they use to bundle money directly to members of Congress, a channel that gives corporate interests preferred access to the lawmakers who regulate them. That interest runs against voters' interest in a political system less pre-shaped by corporate money.

Corporate PACs are significant fee-generating clients for fundraising consultants and party committees, which would lose that revenue. The bill would not eliminate the industry, since super PACs and other channels remain open.
